#Unit 6 — Digitalization in Nepalese Perspective

Lecture hours 7
Marks carried in 2026 paper 22 — one 2-marker (A10 e-governance definition), one 20-marker (D22 Agro-tech Concern case: issues, opportunities, revenue model, policy)
Difficulty ★★★★☆ — the case is compulsory, 20 marks, and the only place a Nepali example is mandatory. You must cite the six case facts and apply Units 1–5 concepts.
Exam yield 🔴 owns the case — 7 hours, 22 marks, and the case is the single biggest differentiator in the paper
Prerequisite Units 1–5 (every concept in the case answer comes from earlier units)
Syllabus bullets E-governance: concepts, process, and structure · E-governance practices in Nepal · Digital financial inclusion in Nepalese financial markets · Opportunities and challenges for digital transformation in the public sector · Digital transformation and the economic performance in trade, tourism, agriculture, and SMEs

Read this first: this unit is the case unit. The 20-mark case (D22) is compulsory — there is no choice. The case narrative gives you six facts (reach, price transparency, data reliability, funding dependency, digital divide, policy). Your answer must cite each fact and apply the concepts from Units 1–5 (4IR, digital transformation drivers, platform economics, asymmetric information, digital currencies, IP, Privacy Act). A generic case answer that does not use the six facts and does not name-drop earlier units will fail.

#6.1 E-governance — concepts, process, and structure

E-governance (electronic governance) is the application of information and communication technologies (ICT) to transform the structures, processes, and relationships of government — with the goals of improving service delivery, increasing transparency and accountability, enabling citizen participation, and reducing corruption.

It has three dimensions (the "concepts, process, and structure" the syllabus names):

Dimension What it means Nepal illustration
Concepts (the what) G2C (government-to-citizen), G2B (government-to-business), G2G (government-to-government), G2E (government-to-employee) — the four interaction types Nagarik (G2C: digital ID, certificates); connectIPS (G2B: tax, customs, licence fees); X-Road pilot (G2G: data exchange); e-attendance (G2E)
Process (the how) digitisation → digitalisation → digital transformation: (1) paper to digital, (2) process re-engineering, (3) organisational and business model change most Nepali ministries are at stage 1 (digitisation: PDF forms, basic portals); Nagarik/connectIPS are stage 2 (process re-engineering); no ministry is at stage 3 yet
Structure (the architecture) the technical and institutional stack: (1) digital infrastructure (broadband, data centres, cloud), (2) shared platforms (digital ID, payments, data exchange, document management), (3) applications (sectoral portals, services), (4) governance (policy, standards, security, privacy, capacity) (1) National Data Centre, Ntc/Ncell 4G; (2) Nagarik, connectIPS, X-Road, Mero Kitta; (3) Mero Kitta (land), Nagarik (certificates), DoL (labour), DoI (industry); (4) Digital Nepal Framework, IT Bill, Privacy Act 2075, Cybersecurity Bylaw 2077

#A10 · "What is e-governance?" [2]

Shape: definition + three dimensions + one illustration each. ~55 words.

E-governance is the application of ICT to transform government structures, processes, and relationships — improving service delivery, transparency, accountability, participation, and reducing corruption. It has three dimensions: concepts — G2C, G2B, G2G, G2E interaction types (e.g., Nagarik for G2C, connectIPS for G2B); process — digitisation → digitalisation → digital transformation (most Nepali ministries at stage 1); structure — infrastructure (National Data Centre), shared platforms (Nagarik, connectIPS, X-Road), applications (Mero Kitta, DoL), governance (Digital Nepal Framework, Privacy Act 2075).

(58 words)

#6.2 E-governance practices in Nepal

The syllabus asks for "practices" — these are the live implementations you cite as evidence in the case answer and in any e-governance question.

Practice What it does Status (2026) Relevance to Agro-tech Concern case
Nagarik App digital national ID, birth/death/marriage certificates, voter registration, social security 2M+ downloads; the de facto digital ID backbone farmer identity verification for subsidies, insurance, market access
connectIPS unified payment gateway for government revenue (tax, customs, fees, licences) mandatory for all govt payments; 100+ banks connected fee collection for agri-services; subsidy disbursement
Mero Kitta online land records, ownership certificates, mutation, revenue payment 30+ land revenue offices onboarded; digitising legacy records land collateral for agri-loans; tenure security for farmers
X-Road pilot data exchange layer between government systems (Estonia model) pilot phase; NRB, MOF, MOICS, NID participating interoperability: farmer data across agriculture, finance, local govt
Digital Nepal Framework (2019) 8 sectors, 80 initiatives: digital foundation, agriculture, health, education, tourism, finance, urban, governance implementation uneven; some initiatives delivered (Nagarik, connectIPS), many stalled the policy umbrella — the case's "policy measures" question asks to operationalise this
IT Bill (under discussion) legal framework for digital signatures, cybercrime, data protection, e-commerce, intermediary liability not yet enacted; Privacy Act 2075 exists separately the case's "policy measures" needs this law for legal certainty
Cybersecurity Bylaw 2077 critical information infrastructure protection, incident reporting, CERT CERT-Nepal operational; bylaw enforced for banks/telecoms data reliability in the case — price data integrity needs cybersecurity

For the exam: you do not need to memorise every portal. You need to name 3–4, say what they do, and link them to the case (farmer identity, fee collection, land collateral, data exchange, policy framework).

#6.3 Digital financial inclusion in Nepalese financial markets

Digital financial inclusion is the use of digital technologies (mobile money, digital banking, agent banking, fintech) to extend financial services — payments, savings, credit, insurance, investment — to the unbanked and underbanked.

#The Nepal landscape (2026)

Channel Scale / key players What it enables for the case
Mobile wallets eSewa (10M+ users), Khalti, IME Pay, Prabhu Pay — P2P, bill pay, merchant QR, government payments farmer payments, input purchases, subsidy receipt
Agent banking 10,000+ agents (banks + MFIs) — cash-in/cash-out, account opening, loan repayment last-mile access in hill/mountain districts (the case's "near-zero reach")
Digital banking all commercial banks have mobile apps; neobank pilots (e.g., Kosh, Mero Banking) credit scoring from transaction history; paperless loans
Fintech lending alternative credit scoring (telco CDR, wallet transactions, psychometric) — Hamro Patro, Karja, Saarthi smallholder loans without land collateral; the case's "funding model" gap
Insurtech parametric (weather-index) pilots — Beema Samiti + private insurers + NGOs crop insurance linked to satellite/weather data; the case's "risk" gap
Remittance digitisation IME, Prabhu, Himalayan, banks — direct to wallet/bank, QR collection reduces cost, increases formal flow; household income stability

Key statistic (pattern, not audited): ~65% of adults have at least one digital financial account (wallet or bank); ~35% use it actively (monthly). The gap is usage depth — most accounts are for remittance receipt or government payment, not daily financial management.

For the case: the Agro-tech Concern's "NPR 16m fee revenue vs NPR 489m transactions" implies a 0.3% take rate — far below what a sustainable fintech needs. The answer must propose: higher take rate on value-added services (credit, insurance, market linkage), not just transaction fees, and partnerships with the channels above (wallets for payment, agent banking for reach, fintech lending for farmer credit).

#6.6 The Agro-tech Concern case — worked answer for D22 [20 marks ≈ 750 words]

Shape: four sub-parts (a–d), each 150–200 words, each citing case facts + unit concepts. ~750 words total.

#D22(a) · Identify the major issues in the given case.

The Agro-tech Concern case reveals six structural issues, each traceable to a digital-economy mechanism:

  1. Reach gap (digital divide). "Near-zero reach in remote hill and mountain districts" — the platform requires smartphone + data connectivity, which the poorest farmers lack. This is Unit 1's 4IR challenge: digital divide = development divide, and Unit 4's driver 1 (changing customer expectations) failing for the excluded.
  2. Price transparency with data reliability failure. "16% average price gain for dashboard users" proves information asymmetry reduction (Unit 5: adverse selection reduced by price signals). But "manual price collection with errors" means the signal is noisy — Unit 5's platform moral hazard: the platform cannot verify the data it publishes, so trust decays.
  3. Funding model dependency. "Dependent on UNDP, SDC, ministry subsidies earning only NPR 16 million a year in fees" against "NPR 489 million in direct transactions" = a 0.3% take rate. Unit 3's value finance is broken: the platform captures value only from transaction fees, not from the value it creates (credit, insurance, logistics, market linkage).
  4. Farmer onboarding and identity. 85,555 registered farmers — but are they verified? Unit 6.1's Nagarik/connectIPS/Mero Kitta are the identity/payment/land rails that could verify farmers, enable credit scoring, and de-risk lending. The case does not mention integration.
  5. Sustainability of the peer-to-peer model. "Peer-to-peer knowledge sharing" relies on unpaid contributions (Unit 3: generative platform needs incentive design). Without reputation rewards or monetisation, quality and participation will decay.
  6. Policy vacuum. No legal framework for agri-data ownership, agri-fintech licensing, platform liability for price errors, or subsidy distortion. Unit 1's regulatory challenges and Unit 6.1's IT Bill / Privacy Act 2075 gaps are the root cause.

#D22(b) · Evaluate the opportunities and challenges of digital transformation in the agriculture sector in Nepal using the example of Agro-tech Concern.

Opportunities (three, with case evidence):

  1. Leapfrogging extension services. The platform delivers weather advisories and price data to 85,555 farmers without a single government extension officer visiting a hill village. This is Unit 4's driver 4 (cloud elasticity) and Unit 1's 4IR leapfrogging — digital reaches where physical infrastructure does not.
  2. Market efficiency and farmer income. The 16% price gain for dashboard users is direct evidence that information asymmetry reduction (Unit 5) translates to income. NPR 489m in direct transactions bypasses middlemen — Unit 3's platform/marketplace model capturing value from matchmaking.
  3. Financial inclusion gateway. Registered farmers are a de-risked pool for lenders. With Nagarik identity, Mero Kitta land records, and wallet transaction history, fintechs can offer parametric insurance and input credit (Unit 6.3). The platform becomes the data intermediary (Unit 5) that solves the adverse selection problem for agricultural finance.

Challenges (three, with case evidence):

  1. Infrastructure and the digital divide. Near-zero reach in hill/mountain districts means the farmers who need the price gain most are excluded. Unit 1's 4IR challenge: digital divide = development divide — the platform deepens inequality unless paired with agent banking (Unit 6.3) and offline-first design.
  2. Data integrity and trust. Manual price collection with errors undermines the platform's core value proposition. Unit 5's platform moral hazard — the platform publishes prices it cannot verify; farmers lose trust; the 16% gain evaporates. Automated price feeds (APIs from wholesale markets, satellite imagery) are the fix.
  3. Business model unsustainability. NPR 16m fees on NPR 489m transactions = 0.3% take rate. Unit 3's value finance fails: the platform captures only transaction fees, not the value created (credit, insurance, logistics, premium market access). Donor dependency (UNDP, SDC) means the platform optimises for reporting metrics (registered users) not unit economics.

#D22(c) · Suggest the sustainable revenue model that can be followed by Agro-tech Concern to support farmers in the digitalization of agri-business.

Shift from "transaction-fee only" to a "platform ecosystem revenue stack" — four layers:

Layer Revenue stream Mechanism Why it fits Agro-tech
1. Marketplace commission (core) 1.5–2.5% on facilitated transactions (not all NPR 489m — only where platform matches buyer/seller) standard marketplace model (Unit 3) raises take rate from 0.3% to ~2% on matched volume; aligns with value delivered
2. Financial services partnership (high margin) referral fees / revenue share from: (a) input credit (fintech lending), (b) parametric crop insurance, (c) equipment leasing Unit 6.3 (digital financial inclusion); Unit 5 (asymmetry reduction via platform data) platform's farmer data de-risks lending/insurance; partners pay for qualified leads
3. Premium analytics & market intelligence (SaaS) subscription from: (a) traders/processors (demand forecasts), (b) input companies (regional demand), (c) government/NGOs (policy dashboards) Unit 3 (data/attention model → B2B SaaS); Unit 4 (data as strategic asset) the 85k farmers + transaction history = proprietary agri-data asset
4. Logistics & fulfilment enablement fee per shipment for integrated logistics (cold chain, aggregation, last-mile) via 3PL partners Unit 4 (platform/ecosystem economics); Unit 6.3 (agent banking for last-mile) solves the "manual price collection" gap — automated collection at aggregation points

Governance condition: all revenue layers require farmer consent and data rights compliance (Privacy Act, 2075 — Unit 1). The platform must be a trusted data intermediary, not a data extractor.

#D22(d) · What types of policy measures would you suggest to the Ministry of Agriculture for enabling e-governance platforms to be effectively implemented in agri-business digitalization?

Four policy pillars, each citing a Unit 6.1 e-governance practice:

  1. Digital public infrastructure (DPI) for agriculture — mandate integration. Require all agri-platforms (public and private) to integrate with Nagarik (farmer identity), connectIPS (subsidy/fee payments), Mero Kitta (land collateral), and X-Road (inter-ministerial data exchange). Rationale: the case's farmer onboarding, subsidy delivery, and credit scoring all fail without these rails. Unit 6.1 structure: shared platforms layer.
  2. Agri-data governance framework — ownership, standards, liability. Enact rules for: (a) farmer data ownership (farmer owns their production/transaction data; platform is processor), (b) price data standards (automated feeds from wholesale markets, not manual collection), (c) platform liability for erroneous price signals that cause farmer loss. Rationale: manual price errors (case) and algorithmic opacity (Unit 5) need legal clarity. Unit 6.1 governance layer + Privacy Act 2075.
  3. Blended finance and de-risking for agri-fintech. Create a credit guarantee fund (government + development partners) that backs fintech loans to platform-verified farmers; allow parametric insurance payouts via connectIPS. Rationale: the case's funding dependency (NPR 16m fees) proves the platform cannot finance farmers alone; the state must de-risk the financial inclusion layer. Unit 6.3 digital financial inclusion + Unit 4 value finance.
  4. Capacity and sustainability — shift from project to platform. Replace NGO/project grants with outcome-based contracts: pay the platform for verified farmer income increase, verified transaction volume, verified financial inclusion metrics. Mandate open APIs so other innovators (insurtech, logitech, agri-input) can build on the platform. Rationale: the case's "UNDP/SDC/ministry subsidies" are input-based; the platform needs to be a sustainable platform business (Unit 3), not a project. Unit 4 operating model + Unit 6.1 process (digital transformation).

#A10 · "What is e-governance?" [2]

E-governance is the application of ICT to transform government structures, processes, and relationships — improving service delivery, transparency, accountability, participation, and reducing corruption. Three dimensions: concepts — G2C, G2B, G2G, G2E (e.g., Nagarik for G2C, connectIPS for G2B); process — digitisation → digitalisation → digital transformation (most Nepali ministries at stage 1); structure — infrastructure (National Data Centre), shared platforms (Nagarik, connectIPS, X-Road), applications (Mero Kitta, DoL), governance (Digital Nepal Framework, Privacy Act 2075).

(58 words)

#D22 · Agro-tech Concern case [20]

(a) Major issues. (1) Reach gap — near-zero reach in hill/mountain districts (Unit 1: digital divide = development divide). (2) Price transparency with data reliability failure — 16% gain proves asymmetry reduction (Unit 5), but manual price errors = platform moral hazard (Unit 5). (3) Funding dependency — NPR 16m fees on NPR 489m transactions = 0.3% take rate; value finance broken (Unit 3). (4) Farmer identity — no Nagarik/connectIPS/Mero Kitta integration for verification/credit (Unit 6.1). (5) Peer-to-peer sustainability — unpaid contributions decay without incentives (Unit 3: generative platform). (6) Policy vacuum — no agri-data ownership, agri-fintech licensing, platform liability framework (Unit 1 regulatory, Unit 6.1 IT Bill).

(b) Opportunities & challenges. Opportunities: (1) Leapfrogging extension — weather/price to 85k farmers without officers (Unit 4 driver 4, Unit 1 4IR leapfrogging). (2) Market efficiency — 16% price gain = asymmetry reduction; NPR 489m direct = marketplace model (Unit 3). (3) Financial inclusion gateway — registered farmers = de-risked pool for fintech via Nagarik/Mero Kitta/wallet data (Unit 6.3, Unit 5). Challenges: (1) Infrastructure divide — hill/mountain exclusion deepens inequality (Unit 1 4IR challenge). (2) Data integrity — manual errors undermine trust; need automated feeds (Unit 5 platform moral hazard). (3) Business model unsustainability — 0.3% take rate, donor-dependent, optimises for metrics not unit economics (Unit 3 value finance).

(c) Sustainable revenue model. Shift to four-layer platform ecosystem revenue stack: (1) Marketplace commission 1.5–2.5% on matched transactions (raises take rate, aligns with value). (2) Financial services partnership — referral/revenue share from input credit, parametric insurance, equipment leasing (platform data de-risks lending; Unit 6.3, Unit 5). (3) Premium analytics SaaS — subscriptions from traders, input companies, government for demand forecasts/regional demand/policy dashboards (Unit 3 data/attention → B2B SaaS). (4) Logistics enablement — fee per shipment for integrated cold chain/aggregation via 3PL partners (Unit 4 ecosystem economics). Governance: farmer consent + Privacy Act 2075 compliance.

(d) Policy measures for Ministry of Agriculture. (1) Mandate DPI integration — all agri-platforms integrate with Nagarik (identity), connectIPS (payments), Mero Kitta (land), X-Road (data exchange) (Unit 6.1 shared platforms). (2) Agri-data governance framework — farmer data ownership (farmer owns, platform processes), price data standards (automated feeds), platform liability for erroneous signals (Unit 6.1 governance + Privacy Act 2075). (3) Blended finance for agri-fintech — credit guarantee fund for platform-verified farmers; parametric insurance via connectIPS (Unit 6.3 + Unit 4 value finance). (4) Outcome-based contracts + open APIs — pay for verified income increase/transaction volume/financial inclusion; mandate open APIs for innovators (Unit 4 operating model, Unit 3 platform business).

(~750 words total across four sub-parts)

#6.8 Traps

Trap Why it costs marks Fix
Writing a generic case answer without citing the six case facts the case gives you the facts — ignoring them loses marks cite all six: 85,555 farmers, NPR 489m transactions, 16% price gain, near-zero hill/mountain reach, manual price errors, NPR 16m fee revenue
Not naming Units 1–5 concepts in the case answer the case is the integration test for the whole subject 4IR, digital transformation drivers, platform economics, value finance, asymmetric information, Privacy Act, digital financial inclusion, e-governance rails
Answering D22(d) with "government should support farmers" vague; the question asks for policy measures for e-governance platforms four pillars: DPI integration, agri-data governance, blended finance, outcome-based contracts
Forgetting the Privacy Act, 2075 in the case answer the only named Nepali law in the syllabus one line in (c) and (d): farmer consent, data rights, purpose limitation
Treating the 0.3% take rate as "low fees are good for farmers" misses the sustainability point — the platform dies value finance must capture created value (credit, insurance, analytics, logistics)
Not linking e-governance practices (Nagarik, connectIPS, Mero Kitta, X-Road) to the case Unit 6.1 is the implementation layer for the case each sub-part cites at least one rail
Writing D22 as one essay instead of four labelled parts the question has four sub-questions (a–d) four labelled parts, each 150–200 words

#6.9 Self-test (answers collapsed)

  1. Define e-governance with its three dimensions (concepts, process, structure). (2 marks — A10)
  2. Name four e-governance practices in Nepal and say what each does. (3 marks)
  3. What is digital financial inclusion? Name three channels in Nepal. (3 marks)
  4. Give three opportunities and three challenges for digital transformation in Nepal's public sector, with Agro-tech illustrations. (5–10 marks)
  5. Name the digital drivers for trade, tourism, agriculture, and SMEs in Nepal. (5 marks)
  6. For the Agro-tech Concern case, list the six major issues. (5 marks — D22a)
  7. What is the sustainable revenue model for Agro-tech Concern? Name the four layers. (5 marks — D22c)
  8. What are the four policy pillars for the Ministry of Agriculture? (5 marks — D22d)
Answers
  1. E-governance = ICT transforming government structures/processes/relationships for service delivery, transparency, accountability, participation, reduced corruption. Concepts: G2C/G2B/G2G/G2E. Process: digitisation → digitalisation → digital transformation. Structure: infrastructure, shared platforms, applications, governance.
  2. Nagarik (digital ID/certificates), connectIPS (govt payments), Mero Kitta (land records), X-Road pilot (data exchange), Digital Nepal Framework (policy), IT Bill (legal), Cybersecurity Bylaw (security). Any four with function.
  3. Use of digital tech to extend financial services to unbanked/underbanked. Channels: mobile wallets (eSewa/Khalti), agent banking (10k+ agents), digital banking (bank apps/neobanks), fintech lending (alt credit scoring), insurtech (parametric), remittance digitisation.
  4. Opportunities: (1) Leapfrogging extension — weather/price to 85k farmers (Unit 4 driver 4). (2) Market efficiency — 16% price gain = asymmetry reduction (Unit 5). (3) Financial inclusion gateway — registered farmers = de-risked pool for fintech (Unit 6.3). Challenges: (1) Infrastructure divide — hill/mountain exclusion (Unit 1 4IR). (2) Data integrity — manual errors = platform moral hazard (Unit 5). (3) Business model unsustainability — 0.3% take rate, donor-dependent (Unit 3 value finance).
  5. Trade: e-commerce, digital payments, digital customs, logistics platforms. Tourism: online booking, digital permits, QR payments, virtual tours. Agriculture: precision farming, price transparency, digital finance, traceability. SMEs: digital marketing, e-commerce storefronts, digital payments, cloud SaaS.
  6. (1) Reach gap (digital divide). (2) Price transparency with data reliability failure. (3) Funding dependency (0.3% take rate). (4) Farmer identity (no Nagarik/connectIPS/Mero Kitta integration). (5) Peer-to-peer sustainability (unpaid contributions decay). (6) Policy vacuum (no agri-data ownership/fintech licensing/platform liability).
  7. Four layers: (1) Marketplace commission 1.5–2.5% on matched transactions. (2) Financial services partnership — referral/revenue share from credit, insurance, leasing. (3) Premium analytics SaaS — subscriptions for demand forecasts, regional demand, policy dashboards. (4) Logistics enablement — fee per shipment for integrated cold chain/aggregation via 3PL.
  8. (1) Mandate DPI integration (Nagarik, connectIPS, Mero Kitta, X-Road). (2) Agri-data governance (farmer data ownership, price standards, platform liability). (3) Blended finance (credit guarantee fund, parametric insurance via connectIPS). (4) Outcome-based contracts + open APIs (pay for verified metrics, mandate open APIs for innovators).
